name: The romantic/heroic antithesis of liberalism
plain_explanation: A rival movement, beginning with Rousseau, that extends individualism from calm intellectual judgment into the realm of passion and self-assertion, glorifying strong emotion, the heroic individual, and rebellion - which Russell argues collapses in practice into dictatorship.
precise_definition: A tradition combining dislike of early industrialism, nostalgia for an idealized Middle Ages, championing of fading aristocratic and Church privilege alongside defense of wage-earners, and vehement assertion of the right of rebellion and the splendor of war, represented philosophically by Fichte, Carlyle, and Nietzsche and poetically by Byron.
why_it_mattered: Russell argues it is self-refuting: since not everyone can be a heroic leader whose individual will prevails, the philosophy in practice produces the despotic rule of the single most successful 'hero,' who then suppresses the very self-assertive ethic by which he rose.
historical_origin: Begins with Rousseau and gains strength from the romantic movement and the principle of nationality.
associated_philosopher: Jean-Jacques Rousseau (originator); Thomas Carlyle, Friedrich Nietzsche, J. G. Fichte (philosophers); Lord Byron (poet)
examples: The 'cult of the hero' as developed by Carlyle and Nietzsche.
objections: Russell's central objection: the theory is 'self-refuting,' since its adoption in practice produces exactly what it claims to oppose - a dictatorial State in which the individual is severely repressed.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell explicitly (if schematically) traces this line 'through Fichte, Byron, Carlyle, and Nietzsche, into Hitler,' contrasted with the 'hard-headed' liberal line running 'through Bentham, Ricardo, and Marx... into Stalin.'
